summary: Defines a schema for representing CORBA object references in an LDAP directory, so distributed applications can find objects through directory lookups. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A phone book lists people so you can call them. This lets a directory list program objects so other programs can find and call them.

how does corba work with ldap
subtitle: A schema for storing CORBA object references in an LDAP directory.

tldr.problem: CORBA applications traditionally use the COS Naming service to find objects, but organizations often deploy LDAP directories for central administration. CORBA applications had no standard way to store and retrieve object references from LDAP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two LDAP object classes (corbaObject and corbaObjectReference) and two attributes (corbaIor for the stringified object reference, and corbaRepositoryId for the interfaces implemented by the object).
tldr.outcome: CORBA applications can now use LDAP as a central repository for object references, interoperably with any LDAP implementation.

today: RFC 2714 is an Informational memo from October 1999. It was created alongside RFC 2713 at Sun Microsystems and remains the standard schema for storing CORBA object references in LDAP directories. The schema is used by CORBA-enabled enterprise systems for service discovery and object registration.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
CORBA (Common Object Request Broker Architecture) is a middleware system that lets programs on different computers call methods on each other's objects. Traditionally, CORBA applications use the COS Naming service to register and discover objects. However, many organizations have deployed LDAP directories as a centralized, replicated naming and directory service. This RFC defines a schema so CORBA applications can store CORBA object references in LDAP directories instead of (or alongside) the COS Naming service.

Like RFC 2713 (Java objects in LDAP), this document provides a common interoperable way to store and retrieve CORBA objects from LDAP. A CORBA application server might register the services it manages in the LDAP directory, so client applications can search for and locate those services by name and properties.
sections.eli5: CORBA programs are on different computers and call each other. They used to find each other using a special naming service. Now they can use a regular directory instead, just like looking someone up in a phone book.

sections.title: CORBA Object References and IORs
sections.content:
A CORBA object reference (or IOR, "Interoperable Object Reference") is an opaque handle that a CORBA client can use to invoke methods on a remote object. The IOR contains enough information for the CORBA runtime to locate and communicate with the object across the network, even if it is running in a different CORBA implementation. The stringified form of an IOR (a text representation) is what gets stored in the directory.

In addition to the IOR, objects have repository IDs (also called "type IDs"), which are unique identifiers for the interfaces the object implements. The RFC defines four standard formats for repository IDs: IDL-style (for CORBA IDL objects), RMI-style (for Java RMI-IIOP remote objects), DCE-style (for DCE/CORBA interoperability), and local (ORB-specific). A single CORBA object may implement multiple interfaces, each with its own repository ID.
sections.eli5: A CORBA object reference is like a phone number: it tells you how to reach an object. The interface is like a business card that says what services the object provides.

sections.title: Object Classes and Attributes
sections.content:
The schema defines three object classes. corbaObject is an abstract base class with two optional attributes: corbaRepositoryId (stores the IDs of all interfaces the object implements) and description (human-readable text). corbaContainer is a structural class used as a dedicated container for a CORBA object entry; it has a mandatory common name (cn). corbaObjectReference is an auxiliary class that adds one mandatory attribute, corbaIor, which stores the stringified interoperable object reference.

To create a directory entry for a CORBA object reference, use javaContainer mixed with corbaObjectReference, or use corbaContainer directly. The corbaIor attribute must contain the stringified form of the IOR, and corbaRepositoryId may contain one or more repository IDs identifying the interfaces.
sections.eli5: The schema has three building blocks. corbaObject is the base. corbaContainer is a container to hold the object. corbaObjectReference is the special part that stores the reference and interfaces.

sections.title: Using CORBA References in LDAP
sections.content:
When a CORBA application wants to register a service, it creates a stringified IOR from its CORBA object, then creates an LDAP entry with the corbaObjectReference class. The entry includes the corbaIor attribute (the stringified reference) and optionally the corbaRepositoryId attribute(s) listing the interfaces. Clients search the directory by name or other attributes to find the service they need.

Because the corbaIor attribute's syntax is IA5 String with case-insensitive matching, the stringified reference is human-readable and searchable. The schema's use of standard LDAP conventions makes CORBA object references compatible with any LDAP directory, and the interoperable object reference format means the reference works across different ORB implementations.
sections.eli5: To register an object, you write down its phone number (the IOR) and what it does (its interfaces) in the directory. To find an object, you search the directory for the service you want, get the phone number, and call it.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
Storing a CORBA object reference in the directory makes the reference available to anyone with directory access, potentially exposing the object to a wider audience than intended. Applications deploying this schema should be aware that storing an IOR in the directory may broaden the set of potential callers. Access control mechanisms in the LDAP server provide the primary way to restrict who can see registered objects.

The schema is fully interoperable because it relies only on standard LDAP attribute types and conventions. Both Java RMI-IIOP (which uses RMI-style repository IDs) and pure CORBA applications (using IDL-style repository IDs) can coexist in the same directory. This schema was developed in parallel with RFC 2713 (Java objects in LDAP) at Sun Microsystems, and the two schemas are complementary.
sections.eli5: Be aware that registering an object in a directory makes it visible to everyone who can read the directory. Use access controls to keep private objects private. The nice thing is that CORBA programs and Java programs can both use the same directory.
